title: The Rupee Is Asia's Worst-Performing Currency This Year. Here Is What Every NRI Should Do About It.
excerpt: Bank of America says the rupee could hit 98 to the dollar by July. For remittances, property, and FCNR deposits, the math has shifted — and the RBI's new incentive windows are temporary.
body:
The Indian rupee has lost more than six per cent of its value against the US dollar this year, making it Asia's worst-performing major currency. Bank of America Securities now warns it could slide to 98 per dollar by July. If you are an NRI, every one of those numbers touches your money in ways that are simultaneously good and bad — and most people are not thinking about it carefully enough.

## What Is Happening to the Rupee

The rupee hit a record low of nearly 97 to the dollar on May 20 and was trading around 95.24 on Friday after the Reserve Bank of India unveiled a package of measures to attract dollar inflows. The currency has been battered by three forces converging at once.

First, the Iran war that began in late February sent crude oil prices surging. India imports nearly 90 per cent of its crude requirements, and every dollar increase in the oil price widens the country's current account deficit and puts pressure on the rupee.

Second, foreign investors have pulled approximately $27 billion out of Indian equities so far in 2026 — surpassing last year's record outflows. That is a massive wave of dollars leaving the country.

Third, the US economy keeps running hotter than expected. The May jobs report showed 172,000 new positions and a steady 4.3 per cent unemployment rate, pushing odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike this year to nearly 70 per cent. A higher US interest rate makes dollars more attractive relative to rupees.

## The RBI's Response

On Friday, the RBI held its benchmark repo rate steady at 5.25 per cent — a decision that surprised no one — but paired it with the most aggressive dollar-mobilisation package since the 2013 taper tantrum.

The measures include a discounted forex swap facility for public sector companies raising external commercial borrowings, a scheme to bear the full hedging cost for banks raising three-to-five-year NRI deposits through September, and an expansion of the Fully Accessible Route to new 15, 30, and 40-year government bonds.

Simultaneously, the Indian government scrapped capital gains tax for foreign holders of government securities — a move aimed squarely at getting India included in more global bond indices and attracting passive foreign capital.

"These measures can aid the rupee's appreciation towards 94 to 94.50 on spot over the near term," said Anindya Banerjee of Kotak Securities, though he noted the upside in USD/INR is now capped around 96.

## What This Means for NRI Money

**Remittances**: If you are sending dollars to India, a weaker rupee is straightforwardly good news. At 95 rupees per dollar, a $1,000 remittance buys ₹95,000 — compared to ₹83,000 at the start of 2025. That is a 14 per cent bonus in purchasing power for the same outflow. If BofA is right about 98, the window gets even wider.

**Property purchases**: For NRIs considering buying property in India, the math has shifted meaningfully. A flat in Bangalore or Mumbai that costs ₹1 crore now costs roughly $105,000 at current rates, down from $120,000 eighteen months ago. The RBI's rate hold also means home loan rates in India remain stable, which helps if you are financing locally.

**FCNR deposits**: The RBI's new incentives for Foreign Currency Non-Resident deposits make this an unusually attractive moment to park dollars in Indian banks. With the central bank bearing hedging costs through September, the effective yield on these deposits improves. The catch: this window is explicitly temporary.

**Returning to India**: If your plan is to eventually move back, a weak rupee cuts both ways. Your dollar savings buy more in India, but if you are still earning in rupees or have rupee-denominated assets, their dollar value has fallen. The longer the rupee stays weak, the more this matters.

**India investments**: The RBI and government have doubled the amount NRIs can invest in Indian equities and scrapped taxes on foreign bond investments. If you believe the rupee will recover — and most economists expect it will once oil prices normalise — buying Indian assets at current exchange rates locks in a discount.

## The Bigger Picture

Prime Minister Modi has taken the unusual step of urging citizens to conserve foreign exchange, asking people to avoid unnecessary foreign travel and work from home to reduce fuel consumption. India has raised gold import duties to 15 per cent and tightened silver import rules. These are not small gestures — they signal genuine concern at the highest levels about the country's external balance.

David Hauner of BofA Securities does not expect an immediate rate hike but forecasts 25-basis-point increases in both October and December, taking the repo rate to 6 per cent by year-end. Capital Economics is more aggressive, projecting a cumulative 75-basis-point hike to 6 per cent.

For NRIs, the practical takeaway is straightforward: if you have been delaying remittances, property decisions, or FCNR deposits, the current exchange rate is the most favourable it has been in years — and the RBI's temporary incentive windows add an extra layer of urgency. The rupee may recover, or it may fall further. But the asymmetry right now favours action over waiting.
